title: Stellar Snowflakes
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6441, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6441 · constellation Scorpius · about 13000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The stars of NGC 6441 glitter like snowflakes in this Hubble view. This globular cluster sits about 13,000 light-years from the center of the Milky Way. As with snowflakes, the exact number of stars is hard to pin down.

Together, its stars are estimated to weigh 1.6 million times as much as the Sun. By that measure, NGC 6441 counts among the heaviest and brightest of our galaxy's globular clusters. It hosts four pulsars, spinning stellar remnants that each complete a rotation in a few milliseconds.

Also hidden in the cluster is JaFu 2, a planetary nebula. Despite the name, planetary nebulae have little to do with planets. They are a stage in the lives of intermediate-mass stars, lasting only a few tens of thousands of years, a mere moment on astronomical timescales.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.40 x 2.42 arcminutes) and distance (13000 light years), the frame spans roughly 9.1 × 9.2 light-years. Its light set out about 13,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The image combines ultraviolet and visible observations from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of this image records ultraviolet light, which is invisible to the human eye.

explore: The Milky Way has about 150 known globular clusters. They contain some of the first stars a galaxy produces, yet exactly how they formed and evolved remains unclear to astronomers.
